newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraqi wants to meet UN arms expectations this year.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi wants to meet UN arms expectations this year.

text.p: A senior Iraqi official said on Wednesday his government was determined to comply with U.N. disarmament requirements this year despite what he considered unfair criticisms from weapons inspectors.

Riyadh al-Qaysi, undersecretary in Iraq's foreign ministry, was in New York speaking to Security Council members on the latest report from the U.N. Special Commission in charge of ridding Iraq of dangerous weapons.

"Whether we see a light at the end of the tunnel, that is again specuation," al-Qaysi told reporters. "What we know is that we should complete, finalise work on our commitments and we are determined to do so this year and then we see how the situation develops."
A clean bill of health is necessary from the U.N. commission before sanctions, in particular the oil embargo, imposed on Iraq in 1990 can be lifted entirely.
The commission's latest half-year report, released last Friday, said it was still missing documentation on Iraq's nuclear, biological, chemical and ballistic missile programmes.

In particular it said Iraq was obstructing a long-term monitoring system to make sure it did not reacquire the dangerous arms. It called on President Saddam Hussein's government to make a political decision and give up "once and for all, all capabilities and ambition to retain" the weapons.
In response, al-Qaysi said the report rehashed old material and exaggerated the problems.
"What we have acheived, which is any measure not small, is being dumped with old stories of the past," he said.
He noted that Iraqi personnel were not always able to comply with U.N. requests on short notice.
"We are a Third World country...short of staff, short of technique, short of equipment," he said, adding that Iraq's political commitment was obvious in work accomplished so far.
Al-Qaysi said he believed many people in the world felt sanctions, imposed on Iraq after its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait, had gone on for too long.
"As far as I can sense the feeling in the Arab world as a whole, non-governmental circles and a vast majority of governmental circles are saying enough is enough," he said.

He said U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was moving the goal posts. He noted that her recent speech on Iraq urged Baghdad to comply with all U.N. resolutions but at the same time warned that sanctions would not be lifted as long as President Saddam Hussein was in power.

Al-Qaysi also complained about delays in distributing the proceeds of the "oil-for-food" deal, an exception to the sanctions that allows Iraq to sell up to $2 billion of oil over six months for food and other humanitarian goods.

"We are not happy at all with the delays that are being pressed in this particular field, especially by the United States. We pumped the allowable amound of oil, the United Nations got its expenses and the Iraq population has not benefitted from the deal," he said.
First food deliveries have arrived in Iraq, with some shipments working through a complicated distribution and monitoring system to get to the Iraqi people.
